synopsis: Across the synthesis, simulation-credibility chapter and glossary, the central rule is to separate tuning, validation or confirmation, and untouched audit data; data used to judge the system must not have helped build or tune it [f135, f7589, f6992, f14471]. Splits should hold out whole sites, weather episodes, machine identities or scenario families rather than random frames, because adjacent frames shared between tuning and validation create severe leakage [f137, f6990, f6991, f14327]. The release-rate claim must rest on a frozen, stratified random sample from the declared operating-domain distribution, drawn before tuning; fixed seeds and content hashes protect its identity, and full-set evaluation is reserved for release candidates [f14131, f14298, f7134]. Audit governance limits the tuning team to aggregate pass/fail results, prohibits optimizing against audit failures, and requires contaminated cases to be retired and replaced; tuned-versus-frozen performance should be reported because a large gap signals over-fitting [f6954, f7135, f6953, f14313]. Physical-model credibility requires frozen calibration challenged on independent boundary conditions, while using every physical case for tuning leaves no untouched predictive evidence; the cited 2017 expert-weighting cross-validation study likewise found strong in-sample performance with an out-of-sample penalty [f6167, f8225, f9946].
